c.tagline: Honduras's industrial powerhouse and gateway to the Copán ruins and the Caribbean coast.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are uncommon; agree the fare before getting in. Shared colectivo taxis run fixed routes for a set fare, while ride-hailing apps give an up-front price and are the easiest option for visitors.

emergency.note: 911 is the unified national emergency number connecting to police, fire, and ambulance.

hood_landmark.Barrio El Centro: San Pedro Cathedral, San Pedro Sula
hood_landmark.Barrio Los Andes: Estadio Francisco Morazán, San Pedro Sula

avoid.reason: Elevated violent crime; avoid outer neighborhoods, caution downtown

hood_desc: The downtown core laid out in quadrants around the Parque Central, the 1949 San Pedro Cathedral, the Museo de Antropología e Historia, and the main commercial streets; best for first-timers who want the historic sights and business district within walking distance, though it empties out and quiets down after dark.

The city's hotel, dining, and nightlife strip along and inside Avenida Circunvalación, home to international chain hotels, shopping malls, casinos, bars, and restaurants; the safest and most convenient base for most visitors.

An upscale, leafy residential neighborhood just northwest of the center near the river, with quiet streets, private homes, and a handful of boutique hotels; suits travelers wanting calm close to downtown.
A large residential and commercial district in the south with major shopping centers, supermarkets, and hotels near City Mall; a practical, modern base away from the old center.
A traditional working residential barrio north of the center near the Estadio Francisco Morazán, with local markets and eateries; an authentic, budget-friendly, everyday-life feel.

water.note: Drink bottled or purified water only.

transit.hours: City buses and rapiditos generally run from around 5:00 AM to 8:00 PM; after dark, taxis and ride-hailing apps fill the gap.
transit.note: San Pedro Sula has no metro, tram, or commuter rail. Public transport is a network of city buses and rapiditos (shared minibuses on fixed routes), supplemented by taxis, colectivos, and ride-hailing apps. Most visitors rely on Uber, InDrive, or hotel-arranged transport rather than local buses.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash (lempiras) directly to the driver on board; there is no rechargeable transit card system.

bus: Gran Central Metropolitana terminal to Tegucigalpa, La Ceiba, Copán, and other cities

transit.m: Local bus along the La Lima highway toward downtown (infrequent, ~40 min)

tip.r: A 10% service charge is often added to restaurant bills; if not, leaving around 10% is customary. Rounding up is common for taxis.

landmarks: Catedral Metropolitana San Pedro Apóstol
The city's neocolonial landmark cathedral, begun in 1949, raises its stately columned facade over the palm-lined central park.
Parque Central (Plaza Municipal)
San Pedro Sula's bustling civic heart, alive with vendors, shoeshiners and street preachers beneath the cathedral's gaze.
Museo de Antropología e Historia
The best introduction to the Sula Valley's past, tracing pre-Columbian Maya-influenced cultures through to the banana-boom era.
Mercado Guamilito
A sensory artisan market stacked with hammocks, Lenca pottery and cigars, famous for its baleada stalls serving Honduras's favourite snack.
Parque Nacional Cusuco
A cloud-forest reserve in the Merendón mountains above the city, sheltering quetzals, toucans and dwarf forest along misty trails.
Cascadas de Pulhapanzak
Honduras's most spectacular waterfall thunders 43 metres beside ancient ceremonial mounds, with a daring guided walk behind the curtain.
Lago de Yojoa
The country's largest natural lake, a birdwatching paradise of over 480 species ringed by mountains, coffee farms and lakeside fish restaurants.
Fortaleza de San Fernando de Omoa
An imposing 18th-century Spanish coastal fortress near the Caribbean, built to fend off pirates raiding colonial silver shipments.
Museo de la Naturaleza
A family-friendly natural-history collection of Honduran wildlife, geology and ecosystems, handy for a rainy afternoon in the city.
Cathedral viewpoint at El Merendón
The forested Merendón range flanking the city offers cool-air lookouts and coffee fincas with sweeping panoramas over the Sula Valley.

train.note: There is no scheduled passenger rail service in Honduras. The FNH line from San Pedro Sula to Puerto Cortés survives as a 50 km freight railway carrying mainly timber, and a short commuter and tourist train was set up in the city in 2010, but nothing links San Pedro Sula to Tegucigalpa or to any neighbouring country by rail. Intercity travel is by coach or by air from Ramón Villeda Morales airport.

intl.to: Guatemala City (Guatemala), San Salvador (El Salvador), Managua (Nicaragua), San José (Costa Rica), Panama City (Panama) & Tapachula (Mexico)

bus.note: San Pedro Sula is Honduras's main coach hub and almost everything leaves from the Gran Central Metropolitana de Autobuses, a large modern terminal about 4-5 km south-east of the centre with all the domestic and international lines under one roof. Alongside Tica Bus, Hedman Alas runs premium services to Tegucigalpa, La Ceiba, Copán Ruinas and on to Guatemala City and Antigua, and King Quality covers San Salvador and Guatemala City; tickets are bought at the terminal counters or on the operators' websites. Guatemala City is around 7-8 hours via the Corinto or Agua Caliente border and San Salvador about 6-7 hours via El Amatillo or El Poy, with immigration handled at the frontier while the coach waits. The CA-4 agreement between Honduras, Guatemala, El Salvador and Nicaragua means most nationalities move between them on a single 90-day entry, but passports are still stamped.

intl.to: Placencia & Big Creek/Mango Creek (Belize) - sails from Puerto Cortés, about 1 hr north of San Pedro Sula
intl.op: small licensed Honduran boat operators — tickets bought at the Puerto Cortés dock

ferry.note: San Pedro Sula is inland; the nearest port is Puerto Cortés, roughly 60 km north and an hour by bus or taxi. From there a small weekly passenger boat has long run across to Placencia and Big Creek in southern Belize, usually leaving on a Monday and returning Friday, but it is a modest open boat, weather-dependent and frequently suspended, so confirm locally before travelling and get your Honduran exit stamp at the Puerto Cortés immigration office first. There is no scheduled ferry to Roatán or the other Bay Islands from Puerto Cortés - those sail from La Ceiba. Cruise ships call at Puerto Cortés but do not sell point-to-point passage.

half.name: Tela
half.blurb: A Caribbean coastal town with Garífuna communities and beaches, gateway to the Punta Sal wildlife refuge along the Bay of Honduras.

half.name: Puerto Cortés
half.blurb: Honduras's main deep-water port on the Caribbean, with a long public beach and modest colonial-era buildings along the waterfront.

full.name: Copán Ruinas
full.blurb: A Maya archaeological site near the Guatemalan border famous for its carved stelae and a hieroglyphic stairway recording centuries of dynastic history.
